deep.reconstruction:
The page is a blank printed commercial form (columns No. der Karte / Zeichen / Stück / Pfund / Loth) that Riemann reused for scrap. The writing is upside down relative to the form, in pencil, in German Kurrent. It is heavily struck through and largely illegible at this resolution, with red-pencil additions on some sketches. No formulas or computations appear.

What can be made out, reading the page turned the right way up:
(a) A sequence of numbered entries, marked I, II, III (Roman) and '4.' (Arabic). Each is headed by a short phrase that appears to read '... zusammenhängende Fläche' ('...-connected surface'). The ordinal words before it are not legible in the transcription. My tentative reading is that they say einfach / zweifach / dreifach ('simply / doubly / triply' connected) and so on.
(b) Each entry has an illustrative sketch:
  - a single small closed curve (a simply connected disc);
  - a set of concentric circles, partly drawn in red (an annulus, the standard doubly connected surface, with a closed curve going round the hole);
  - two adjacent discs, each surrounded by red concentric curves and labelled a and b (a region with two holes, i.e. triply connected, with two independent non-bounding closed curves a and b);
  - an oval enclosing two loops that cross, again with red curves labelled a and b. This most plausibly shows how a closed curve, or a pair of curves, does or does not bound a part of the surface. That is the criterion behind the 1857 definition of connectivity.
(c) Several lines of prose, mostly cancelled, presumably explaining each example. They appear to say how many cuts (Querschnitte), or how many closed curves that together fail to bound, the surface admits.

Context: the next page (155r) continues with the remark that an (n+1)-fold connected surface 'can now be defined' as one cut into a simply connected surface by n cross-cuts, 'as I did in my Dissertation'. It adds that one must then prove that every other system of n cross-cuts does the same. Riemann compares this with the definition 'chosen in the preceding paper'. That is the 1857 'Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen', where connectivity is defined through systems of closed curves that do not bound. He gives reasons for preferring the 1857 definition: it arises directly from the study of periodicity, and it simplifies the proofs.

The present page is therefore a draft or illustration sheet for this remark on analysis situs: a list of examples of surfaces of increasing connectivity with pictures. In modern terms, a planar region with k holes has connectivity k+1 = 2 - chi, where chi is the Euler characteristic, and becomes simply connected after k cross-cuts.

No derivation is present to reconstruct step by step. The identification of the ordinals and the purpose of the a, b labels is mine and tentative.

results.what: Examples of planar surfaces of connectivity 1, 2, 3 (and 4): a disc, an annulus (concentric circles), and a region with two holes carrying closed curves a and b. These illustrate the definition of multiple connectivity by non-bounding closed curves or by cross-cuts.
results.modern_name: Connectivity of surfaces (first Betti number; connectivity = 2 - Euler characteristic for surfaces with boundary); cutting a surface into a simply connected one
results.usually_credited_to: Bernhard Riemann (Dissertation 1851; Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen 1857)

results.what: Implicit comparison (completed on the next page) of two definitions of (n+1)-fold connectivity: by n cross-cuts versus by systems of non-bounding closed curves. This includes the remark that the cross-cut definition requires proving the number of cuts is independent of the choice of cuts.
results.modern_name: Topological invariance of the number of cross-cuts (rank of H_1)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851/1857; rigorous treatment later by C. Neumann, Jordan, and others

deep.surprise_reason: This is a scratch illustration sheet for Riemann's own well-known analysis-situs concepts (connectivity, cross-cuts) from his 1851 dissertation and 1857 Abelian functions paper. It has mild interest as a draft of an unpublished comparison of the two definitions, but contains no new mathematics.

checkable.sympy: k = symbols('k', integer=True, nonnegative=True); chi = 1 - k; simplify((2 - chi) - (k + 1)) == 0
checkable.asserts: A planar disc with k holes has Euler characteristic 1-k and connectivity 2-chi = k+1. So the annulus (k=1) is doubly connected and the two-hole region (k=2) is triply connected.

checkable.sympy: n = symbols('n', integer=True, nonnegative=True); chi0 = 1 - n; simplify(chi0 + n - 1) == 0
checkable.asserts: Each cross-cut raises the Euler characteristic by 1. Thus n cross-cuts reduce an (n+1)-fold connected surface (chi = 1-n) to a simply connected one (chi = 1).
A closed surface of genus g with one boundary hole (chi = 1-2g) has connectivity 2g+1, Riemann's (2p+1)-fold connected T'.
